clue.text: Supporting that man with no money in Bow (6)

indicators.note: Something with no money has had the letter for money taken away.
What is put in something sits inside it, so the shortened man goes inside the bow.

blocks.note: to bow is to bend at the waist; this word opens to take the rest
that man, as an object, is him
M is a standard abbreviation for money

explanation.surface: A man left penniless in Bow, a district of East London, being propped up by someone.
explanation.walkthrough: Bow looks like the London district in the East End, which its capital letter encourages; it is the verb, to bend at the waist.
explanation.definitionFit: To be behind someone is to support them, as in 'we're all behind you'.

clue.text: Tired soldiers leaving invigorated for duty (9)

indicators.note: Soldiers leaving a word walk out of it, so their letters come out.
One thing given for another is exchanged for it, so the duty takes the soldiers' place.

blocks.note: invigorated means given energy, energised
GIs are American soldiers
VAT, value added tax, is a duty charged on goods in Britain

explanation.surface: Worn-out soldiers going off duty, though they had been feeling full of life.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads 'leaving for duty' as troops setting off; the swap turns ENERGISED into its own opposite. VAT is the British sales tax.
explanation.definitionFit: Enervated means drained of energy, so tired.

clue.text: Curtailed abuse in part of body's regulatory system (7)

indicators.note: A curtailed word has lost its tail, its last letter.

blocks.note: abuse is INSULT, and cutting its tail leaves INSUL
the word itself, used as letters

explanation.surface: Clipped abuse turning up inside some part of the body's machinery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' looks like a link placing the abuse inside the body; it simply supplies its own two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Insulin is the hormone that regulates blood sugar, one component of the body's regulatory (endocrine) system.

clue.text: Schoolgirl shows contempt for Spooner and runs out? (9)

indicators.note: The Rev. Spooner swapped the opening sounds of words, so the phrase is said as he would say it.

blocks.note: a schoolgirl is a miss; she gives up her M sound and takes the D
to show contempt is to diss someone; this word hands over its D and collects the M

explanation.surface: A schoolgirl sneering at Spooner, the Oxford don famous for tangling his words.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket a batter run out is dismissed, so 'runs out' is what a fielder does to a batter; the question mark flags this example of dismissing.
explanation.definitionFit: Running a batter out is one way a fielding side dismisses them, so 'runs out' is a particular case of dismisses.

clue.text: Audience's impression of cast from seat at The Royal Court (6)

indicators.note: What an audience takes in is what it hears, so the answer is how the word sounds.

blocks.note: cast is the past participle of throw; say that word aloud

explanation.surface: A theatregoer's view of the cast from a seat at the Royal Court, a London theatre.
explanation.walkthrough: The Royal Court is a London theatre, so audience, cast and seat all sound theatrical; here the royal court is a monarch's, and 'cast' is the past tense of throw.
explanation.definitionFit: The chair of state a sovereign sits on when holding court, so a plain description of the royal seat.

clue.text: School society exempt from tax (5)

indicators.note: Something exempt from a word is left out of it, so the society's letter is taken away.

blocks.note: to tax something is to strain it, as in taxing your patience
S is an abbreviation for society

explanation.surface: A school society that has charitable status and pays no tax.
explanation.walkthrough: 'School society' reads as one noun phrase; 'School' is the verb, and 'tax' is the verb strain rather than a levy.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym for the verb: to school a pupil or a horse is to instruct and drill it.

clue.text: Round figure in short formula represented capacity of cell? (7)

indicators.note: A word cut short has lost its last letter.
The round figure goes in with the other letters before they are rearranged.
Something re-presented is presented again in a new form, so the letters are rearranged.

blocks.note: a round figure is a circle, the letter O (or a zero)
formula without its last letter

explanation.surface: A mathematical formula, with a round number, used to work out how much a cell can hold.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a biology or battery cell and a calculation; the cell is a room, as in a prison or monastery, and the question mark admits this is one example.
explanation.definitionFit: A roomful is as much as a room can hold, and a cell is a small room.

clue.text: Peer pressure will ultimately lead to bullying going up (5)

indicators.note: Ultimately means in the end, so each of the two words gives its last letter.
The lead to a word is its front, its first letter.
In a down entry, going up means reading from the bottom, so the letters are reversed.

blocks.note: the last letters of pressure and will
the first letter of bullying
something going, like a show that is running, is on

explanation.surface: Peer pressure among children ends up turning into bullying.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Peer pressure' is a set phrase, so the eye skips past 'Peer' as the definition; it is a member of the nobility, and 'going' is ON rather than part of 'going up'.
explanation.definitionFit: In Britain a peer is a titled aristocrat entitled to sit in the House of Lords, a plain synonym.

clue.text: It's playing the game, in more ways than one (13)

definitions.text: It's playing the game, in more ways than one

blocks.note: the literal reading: taking part in a match, the skill of a sportsman
the idiom playing the game also means behaving fairly, the other sense

explanation.surface: A remark that fair play is what counts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Playing the game' means behaving fairly, which is sportsmanship; it also literally means playing a sport, so the phrase fits the answer in more ways than one, as the clue says.
explanation.definitionFit: Sportsmanship is fair and generous conduct in a game, the spirit of playing the game.

clue.text: Argue primacy of gender reassignment commitment to the end (8,5)

indicators.note: The primacy of something is what comes first in it, its first letter.
That first letter is sent to the end of the whole string.

blocks.note: gender reassignment is a sex change
giving your word is a commitment

explanation.surface: Someone arguing for the importance of committing fully to gender reassignment.
explanation.walkthrough: SEXCHANGEWORD with its first letter S moved to the back gives EXCHANGEWORDS. 'Argue' looks like part of the surface's sentence but is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom: trading angry remarks is what arguing amounts to.

clue.text: Printer reduced resolution in Postscript (5)

indicators.note: A reduced word has been cut down, here to its first three letters.
The shortened word goes in between the letters of the postscript.

blocks.note: PS is the abbreviation for postscript
resolution cut to RES, as in hi-res

explanation.surface: A printer turning down its resolution for a PostScript file.
explanation.walkthrough: PostScript is a printer language, so the surface is all computing; here it is just PS, the note after a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A press is a printer, the machine or the firm that prints.

clue.text: To pursue case is perhaps to fight a lonely fight (6-3)

blocks.note: to shadow someone is to follow them
a box is a case

explanation.surface: Pursuing a legal case as if it were a lonely struggle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Case' suggests a lawsuit but is a container; 'perhaps' concedes that a lonely fight is a playful take on shadow-boxing.
explanation.definitionFit: To shadow-box is to spar against an imaginary opponent, fighting alone.

clue.text: Withdrawal ruins love-making arrangement (9)

indicators.note: Making an arrangement of letters puts them in a new order.

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Pulling out ruins the love-making.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Love-making' reads as one word, but 'love' is fodder and 'making arrangement' the instruction. Withdrawal here is the sense of recoiling from something.
explanation.definitionFit: Revulsion, in an older sense, is a sudden drawing back or withdrawal.

clue.text: Kind of wound attributed to rifle shots (5)

indicators.note: What is attributed to the phrase belongs to it, lying inside its letters.

blocks.note: riFLE SHots

explanation.surface: A wound put down to gunfire.
explanation.walkthrough: The link between wound and rifle shots is so natural that the answer sits unnoticed across the two words.
explanation.definitionFit: A flesh wound is one that does not reach bone or organs, so flesh names a kind of wound.

clue.text: Suppress issue about sex (3,2)

indicators.note: Something about another goes around it.

blocks.note: issue means offspring, such as a son
IT is old slang for sex, or sex appeal

explanation.surface: Keeping a lid on a topic to do with sex.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Issue' looks like a subject for debate; it is offspring. IT for sex appeal is a convention.
explanation.definitionFit: To sit on something is to suppress it, keeping it quiet.

clue.text: Row of benches apparently adapted to new position (7,2)

blocks.note: a settle is a high-backed bench, so a row of them looks fitted with settles
the everyday sense: grown used to a new place or job

explanation.surface: A row of benches moved around to suit a new layout.
explanation.walkthrough: A settle is a high-backed wooden bench, so a room lined with a row of them is, on the face of it, settled in; 'apparently' marks that reading as the setter's invention.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who has settled in has got used to a new job, home or position.

clue.text: Opposing parties could be named thus (4,3,2)

indicators.note: Letters that could be something else can be rearranged into it.

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A suggestion for what two rival sides might be called.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue reads like a cryptic definition, and 'named thus' passes as plain English; it is the fodder, with 'could be' telling you to rearrange it.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom: 'them and us' describes a divide between two opposed groups, so the phrase stands for the parties themselves.

clue.text: Make black hole ultimately after red giant's collapse (9)

indicators.note: When the letters collapse they fall in a new order.
Ultimately means at the end, so the last letter of hole.
The E comes after the rearranged letters.

blocks.note: the letters of red giant rearranged
the last letter of hole

explanation.surface: A red giant star collapsing to form a black hole.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Black hole' is a set phrase in the astronomy picture, but 'black' belongs to the definition and only the end of 'hole' is used.
explanation.definitionFit: Denigrate comes from the Latin for blacken, and it still means to blacken someone's name.

clue.text: Poster's intended target (9)

blocks.note: the surface wants a printed poster on a wall; read it as one who posts a letter
the person named on the envelope

explanation.surface: The audience a poster is aimed at.
explanation.walkthrough: A poster seems to be a printed notice; it is someone who posts a letter, whose target is the addressee.
explanation.definitionFit: The addressee is the person a letter is sent to.

clue.text: Former role exists primarily for the benefit of one side (2,5)

definitions.text: for the benefit of one side

indicators.note: Primarily means first of all, so the first letter of exists.

blocks.note: an ex is a former partner, and ex- means former
an actor's role is a part
the first letter of exists

explanation.surface: A former role that existed mainly to benefit one faction.
explanation.walkthrough: Ex parte is Latin, used in law for a hearing or application made by or for one party only.
explanation.definitionFit: Ex parte means on behalf of, or in the interest of, one side only.

clue.text: Swordsman ultimately conceded to pen (5)

indicators.note: Conceding the ultimate letter gives up the last one.

blocks.note: a swordsman who fights with foil or épée in the sport; drop his last letter

explanation.surface: A swordsman finally giving in to a writer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pen' is the verb, to shut in, not the writing tool the surface wants.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: shutting animals inside a barrier is what penning them means.

clue.text: Crisp ready to be cooked in oil? (7)

definitions.text: ready to be cooked in oil?

blocks.note: crisp in the sense of brittle, easily crumbled

blocks.clueFragment: ready to be cooked in oil?
blocks.note: read as fry plus -able, fit for the pan

explanation.surface: Crisps ready for the fryer.
explanation.walkthrough: The second definition reads the word as fry-able, able to be fried; the question mark admits that is not what it means.
explanation.definitionFit: Friable means easily crumbled, crisp and brittle.

clue.text: Relieve oneself in empty soup pan (5)

indicators.note: An empty word has had its insides removed, leaving only the outer letters.
The relief goes inside those outer letters.

blocks.note: soup emptied leaves S and P
to wee is to urinate, relieve oneself

explanation.surface: Someone relieving themselves into an empty soup pan.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Soup pan' reads as a kitchen pan; 'pan' is the definition, the camera move.
explanation.definitionFit: To pan a camera is to sweep it across a scene.

clue.text: Prevailing attitudes disquiet hospital nurses (5)

indicators.note: To nurse something is to hold it close, so the phrase holds the answer inside.

blocks.note: disquiET HOSpital

explanation.surface: Unease at a hospital where nurses set the tone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nurses' reads as hospital staff; it is the verb, holding the answer inside.
explanation.definitionFit: An ethos is the prevailing spirit or attitudes of a group or place.

clue.text: Sailor's drawing up oath given at sea (7,2)

indicators.note: Letters at sea are all over the place, jumbled.

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A sailor drafting a sworn statement while out at sea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drawing up' suggests writing a document; it is a ship coming to a stop.
explanation.definitionFit: Heaving to is the sailor's term for bringing a vessel to a halt, drawing up.

clue.text: Really didn't feel like breaking the lady’s heart (5)

indicators.note: Breaking the letters apart lets them re-form in a new order.
The heart of a word is its middle.

blocks.note: the word itself
the middle two letters of lady

explanation.surface: Someone who did not want to break a woman's heart.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Breaking the lady's heart' reads as a romantic phrase; the lady gives only her middle letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To hate doing something is really not to feel like it, as in 'I hated to leave'.

clue.text: Came into vacant house, having tried moving home beforehand (9)

indicators.note: A vacant house has nothing inside, leaving only its outer letters.
Letters that are moving shift into a new order.
Home comes before the rest.

blocks.note: someone at home is in
house emptied leaves H and E
the letters of tried rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone who inherited an empty house, having first tried to move home.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface's 'moving home' is a house move; 'moving' works on tried and 'home' gives IN.
explanation.definitionFit: To come into money or property is to inherit it.

clue.text: Committee's not interested in discussion (5)

indicators.note: What is in discussion is spoken, so the answer sounds like the word.

blocks.note: not interested means weary and uninvolved; say that word aloud

explanation.surface: A committee that could not care less about the debate.
explanation.walkthrough: A committee bored by its own discussion is the joke; the answer sounds the same.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a group of directors or examiners who govern or decide together is a committee.

clue.text: College dons orchestrated Dean's rise (6)

indicators.note: Orchestrated letters are arranged into a new order.
Letters that don something put it on, wrapping round it.

blocks.note: the letters of dean's rearranged
C is an abbreviation for college

explanation.surface: College dons engineering the promotion of their dean.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dons' looks like university teachers; it is the verb, putting on. The rearranged DEAN'S wraps around C.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: going up, whether a hill, a throne or a career ladder, is rising.

clue.text: Act comprises these unseemly displays (6)

blocks.note: an act of a play is divided into these
making one is a public show of temper

explanation.surface: An act made up of unbecoming behaviour.
explanation.walkthrough: An act of a play is made up of scenes, and making a scene is a public display of temper.
explanation.definitionFit: Scenes are both the parts of an act and embarrassing public outbursts.
